Fulfillment: Where Adam brought sin and death to all humanity through his disobedience in the garden, Jesus, the second Adam, brings righteousness and life through His obedience, even to death on the cross. In Christ, the image of God marred by the fall is restored and a new humanity is born.
Explanation: Adam was made in God's image and placed as head of creation, yet he fell and his whole family fell with him. Jesus succeeds where Adam failed, resisting temptation, obeying the Father, and rising as the head of a redeemed creation.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Fall; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Fulfillment: God provided one ark, entered by one door, through which Noah and his family were saved from judgment on a sinful world. In the same way, God provides one Savior: all who are in Christ are kept safe through the waters of judgment and brought into new life.
Explanation: The ark pictures salvation in Christ: judgment is real, but God Himself designs the refuge and invites people inside before the storm comes. Peter links the floodwaters to baptism, pointing to a conscience cleansed and a life rescued by Christ's resurrection.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood; The Resurrection

Fulfillment: On Mount Moriah Abraham was ready to offer his beloved son, but God stopped him and provided a substitute. Centuries later, on that same mountain region, God did not spare His own Son: Jesus, the beloved Son of promise, was offered so that we might live.
Explanation: Isaac carried the wood up the mountain just as Jesus carried His cross, and Abraham's words, 'God himself will provide the lamb,' found their full answer in Jesus. The scene teaches both the cost of sin and the wonder of a God who provides the sacrifice Himself.
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; The Crucifixion

Fulfillment: Joseph was betrayed by his brothers for pieces of silver, falsely accused, and lowered into prison, yet God raised him to the right hand of power to save many lives. Jesus was likewise betrayed, rejected by His own people, and humbled to death, then exalted to the Father's right hand to save the world.
Explanation: Joseph's story whispers of Jesus at every turn: the beloved son, the unjust suffering, and the forgiving heart that says, 'You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good.' Joseph fed the hungry with bread in famine; Jesus gives Himself as the bread of life forever.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Jesus; Stephen
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; The Crucifixion

OldTestamentPassage: Exodus 1:22; Exodus 2:1-10; Exodus 3:1-10; Exodus 16; Exodus 32:32; Numbers 12:3; Deuteronomy 18:15-18; Deuteronomy 34:10-12
Fulfillment: God promised a prophet like Moses, and Jesus is that prophet, yet greater. Moses led Israel out of slavery in Egypt and mediated the old covenant; Jesus leads all who trust Him out of slavery to sin and mediates a new and better covenant in His blood.
FulfillmentPassage: Matthew 2:13-15; Matthew 4:2; Matthew 11:29; Matthew 17:1-5; John 1:11; John 6:14; John 6:35; John 7:40; Acts 3:22-23; Acts 7:37; Hebrews 3:1-6
Explanation: Moses and Jesus mirror each other at nearly every turn: both were born under a king's order to kill Hebrew baby boys and were miraculously preserved (Exodus 1-2; Matthew 2); both spent time in Egypt and came out of it (Hosea 11:1; Matthew 2:15); both fasted forty days (Exodus 34:28; Matthew 4:2); both mediated a covenant between God and His people (Exodus 24; Luke 22:20); both interceded for a guilty people, Moses even offering himself for them (Exodus 32:32), while Jesus actually gave Himself (Romans 5:8); both were meek (Numbers 12:3; Matthew 11:29); both taught God's law from a mountain, Sinai and the Sermon on the Mount (Exodus 20; Matthew 5-7); both were rejected by their own people (Exodus 32; John 1:11); both provided bread in the wilderness, manna and the Bread of Life (Exodus 16; John 6:35); both led God's people out of bondage, from Egypt and from sin. Where Moses could only lead Israel to the border of the promised land, Jesus brings His people all the way home. And Moses himself foretold a Prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15), a promise Peter and Stephen applied directly to Jesus (Acts 3:22-23; Acts 7:37).
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Numbers; Deuteronomy; Matthew; John; Acts; Hebrews
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Ten Commandments; Transfiguration

Fulfillment: John the Baptist announced Jesus as 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' and Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb, sacrificed for us. At the cross, not one of Jesus' bones was broken, just as the Passover lamb's bones were to remain unbroken.
Explanation: The blood on the doorposts turned God's judgment aside and set a captive people free to journey toward the promised land. Christ's blood does far more: it cleanses the conscience, frees us from slavery to sin, and marks us as God's own for the journey home.
RelatedEvents: The Passover; The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Crucifixion; The Last Supper

Fulfillment: When the crowds asked for a sign like the manna, Jesus declared that He is the true bread from heaven the Father gives. Whoever ate manna still died, but whoever feeds on Christ by faith receives life that never ends.
Explanation: Manna taught Israel daily dependence: God fed His people morning by morning with bread they did not earn or bake. Jesus feeds our souls the same way, not once but daily, as we come to Him in His word and prayer and find Him enough for today.
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Fulfillment: Jesus explained His own cross with this story: 'Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes may have eternal life in him.' Those who simply looked in faith were healed, and all who look to the crucified Christ are saved.
Explanation: The cure mirrored the curse: the image of the very thing that was killing Israel became, lifted up, the means of life. At the cross, Jesus, made sin for us though He knew no sin, becomes the one we look to for healing from sin's deadly bite.

Fulfillment: John writes that the Word became flesh and 'tabernacled' among us, full of grace and truth. In Jesus, God no longer dwelt behind a curtain in a tent but walked among His people in person, and through Him God's presence now fills His church and one day all creation.
Explanation: Every part of the tabernacle whispered of Christ: the one door, the altar, the lampstand, the bread, and the veil guarding the Holy of Holies. It taught a wandering people that a holy God longs to dwell in their midst, a longing fulfilled when Emmanuel came.
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; The Birth of Jesus

Fulfillment: The mercy seat, sprinkled with blood on the Day of Atonement, was the very place where God met His people and forgave them. Paul uses this same word for Jesus: God presented Christ as a mercy seat, a sacrifice of atonement, received by faith, demonstrating His righteousness and mercy together.
Explanation: Between the cherubim above the ark, judgment and mercy met: the law inside the ark condemned, yet the blood above it covered. In Christ, God's justice and love meet fully at the cross, so sinners can draw near without fear.

Fulfillment: Aaron and his sons entered God's presence on Israel's behalf, bearing the people's names over their hearts, yet they had to offer sacrifices for their own sins first and repeat them year after year. Jesus is our great High Priest forever: sinless, He offered Himself once for all and now always lives to intercede for us.
Explanation: The high priest showed that sinners need a mediator who is both set apart for God and able to sympathize with human weakness. Jesus fulfills both perfectly, so we can approach God's throne of grace with confidence, exactly the anchored hope Hebrews describes.

Fulfillment: The daily and yearly sacrifices taught that sin costs life, yet they could never finally take sin away, so they were offered again and again. Jesus, the perfect Lamb without blemish, offered Himself once for all, and by that single offering He has perfected forever those who are being made holy.
Explanation: Burnt, sin, guilt, and fellowship offerings each highlighted a facet of atonement: substitution, cleansing, forgiveness, and restored fellowship. Christ gathers them all into Himself; where the old system was a shadow that pointed forward, His sacrifice is the substance that settles the debt.

Fulfillment: On the Day of Atonement, Aaron laid both hands on the scapegoat, confessed all Israel's sins over it, and sent it into the wilderness bearing their guilt away, never to return. Jesus bore our sins in His body on the cross, and God removes them from us as far as the east is from the west.
Explanation: The two goats together paint one complete picture: one died for sin, the other carried sin away, showing both forgiveness and removal. In Christ we have both, a sacrifice that pays for guilt and a Savior who takes it so far away it can never be charged to us again.

Fulfillment: Jesus Himself named the sign of Jonah: 'Just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of a huge fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.' Jonah's emergence from the fish pointed to Jesus rising from the grave, and Jesus adds that one greater than Jonah is here.
Explanation: Jonah was, in a sense, given up to death to calm a storm and save sailors, then 'resurrected' to preach repentance to the nations. Jesus truly died to save others, truly rose, and sends a message of repentance far wider than Nineveh, to the ends of the earth.

Fulfillment: God promised David a descendant whose kingdom would endure forever, and Jesus is that Son of David, born in Bethlehem and raised to David's throne by His resurrection. Even David's psalms reach beyond himself: Psalm 22 describes the cross, and Psalm 16 celebrates a Holy One who would not see decay.
Explanation: David was shepherd, singer, and king, a man after God's own heart, yet he also fell grievously and needed mercy. Jesus is David perfected: the Good Shepherd who lays down His life, the righteous King who never fails, whose reign brings the justice and peace David only glimpsed.
RelatedBooks: 1 Samuel; 2 Samuel; Psalms; Matthew; Luke; Acts; Romans
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; Davidic Covenant; The Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Fulfillment: Jesus spoke of His own body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days, and He claimed something greater than the temple was here. Through His resurrection, God's dwelling is no longer a building in Jerusalem but Christ Himself and, in Him, His people built together as a living temple.
Explanation: Built on Mount Moriah, where Abraham once offered Isaac, the temple was the meeting place of heaven and earth, filled with God's glory at its dedication. Christ fulfills it by being the true meeting place, and one day the whole new creation becomes God's temple, with no building needed at all.
RelatedBooks: 1 Kings; 2 Chronicles; Matthew; John; Ephesians; 1 Peter
RelatedEvents: Building of Solomon's Temple; The Binding of Isaac; The Resurrection

Fulfillment: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, appears without genealogy, beginning, or end in Scripture, blessed Abraham, and offered bread and wine. God swore that the coming Messiah would be a priest forever in Melchizedek's order, and Hebrews shows Jesus is that eternal priest-king.
Explanation: Unlike Aaron's priests, who died and were replaced, Melchizedek points to a priesthood that never ends and a king who is also a priest. Because Jesus lives forever in this order, He is able to save completely those who come to God through Him.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Last Supper

Fulfillment: Boaz was a near relative who had both the right and the means to redeem Ruth and Naomi, and he gladly paid the price at the city gate to make Ruth his bride. Jesus is our kinsman-redeemer: truly our brother in the flesh, He paid the full price at the cross to redeem a people for Himself.
Explanation: The Hebrew word goel, redeemer, required kinship, ability, and willingness, and Boaz shows all three with kindness and integrity. Ruth, a foreign widow with nothing, pictures us: welcomed by grace into the family line that would lead, through her own great-grandson David, to Christ.
RelatedPeople: Ruth; Naomi; Boaz; King David; Jesus

Fulfillment: Paul states the identification plainly: Israel 'drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ.' The rock was struck once at God's command so thirsty people could live, and Jesus, struck once at the cross, now pours out living water to all who believe.
Explanation: In a dry wilderness, life flowed from an unlikely place, a smitten rock, by God's grace alone. Christ meets us in our driest seasons the same way: His once-for-all suffering opens an unending supply of the Spirit, so His people never thirst in vain.

Fulfillment: Israel passed through the sea, rescued from Pharaoh's army, on their way from slavery to the promised land, and Paul calls this experience a kind of baptism into Moses. In Christ, believers pass through the waters of baptism into a greater exodus, freed from sin's tyranny and raised to walk in newness of life.
Explanation: The sea that saved Israel destroyed the power that enslaved them; God made a way where there was no way, through water no one could cross alone. Baptism proclaims the same pattern: behind us, a defeated enemy and a buried old life; ahead of us, resurrection life with Christ.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Ten Plagues; The Baptism of Jesus; The Resurrection

Fulfillment: Joshua shares Jesus' very name: Yehoshua, 'the Lord saves,' rendered Yeshua in Jesus' day. Joshua led Israel into the rest of the promised land after Moses could not, and Jesus, our greater Joshua, gives the true and lasting rest that the land could only picture.
Explanation: Hosea's name was changed to Joshua as a declaration that salvation belongs to the Lord, not to human strength. The conquest's victories and the land's rest were real gifts, yet Hebrews insists a greater rest remained, and it is found only in Christ, who leads His people home for good.
RelatedEvents: Crossing the Jordan; The Walls of Jericho

Fulfillment: Isaiah's Servant was despised and rejected, pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, silent before His accusers like a lamb to the slaughter. The Gospels show Jesus fulfilling this chapter phrase by phrase, and the risen Christ Himself explained that the Scriptures spoke of His necessary suffering.
Explanation: Long before Isaiah wrote, Joseph's rejection by his brothers and unjust suffering before his exaltation sketched the same pattern of the righteous one suffering to save others. Isaiah gives that pattern its clearest voice, and in Jesus the Servant's wounds become, as Peter writes, the very means by which we are healed.
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Jesus; Philip
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Fulfillment: Just as Abraham raised the knife, God stopped him and revealed a ram caught by its horns in a thicket, offered in Isaac's place. On that same mountain, Abraham named the place 'The Lord Will Provide,' and God ultimately provided His own Son as the substitute who dies in our place.
Explanation: The ram is a pure picture of substitution: an innocent life taken so the beloved son could walk down the mountain alive and free. At the cross the pattern completes itself, for God's Son was not spared, so that everyone who trusts Him goes free.
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; The Crucifixion

Fulfillment: The heavy veil barred the way into the Holy of Holies, entered only once a year by one man with blood, but at the moment Jesus died the veil was torn in two from top to bottom. Through His flesh, Hebrews says, He opened a new and living way into God's presence for all who believe.
Explanation: The torn veil is God Himself removing the barrier, top to bottom, heaven to earth, not human hands reaching up. It stands behind the blog's anchor verse: our hope enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone before us and holds it secure.

Fulfillment: Israel set apart cities where someone who had killed unintentionally could flee from the avenger and find safety until a fair trial, remaining until the death of the high priest. Hebrews speaks of believers who have 'fled to take hold of the hope set before us,' finding in Christ a refuge no accuser can breach.
Explanation: God built mercy into Israel's justice system, marking refuge cities with open gates and clear roads for desperate people running for their lives. Christ is our city of refuge in full: we flee to Him not because we are innocent, but because He has borne our judgment and His protection never expires.

Fulfillment: Every fiftieth year, trumpets sounded across the land: debts were released, slaves went free, and family land returned to its original owners. Standing in the Nazareth synagogue, Jesus read Isaiah's Jubilee promise, 'to proclaim freedom for the prisoners and good news to the poor,' and announced, 'Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.'
Explanation: Jubilee taught Israel that the land, the people, and even time itself belong to God, and that His economy runs on release rather than accumulation. In Christ, the greater Jubilee has dawned: sins forgiven, captives freed, and an eternal inheritance restored that can never be lost again.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; The Sermon on the Mount

Fulfillment: Balaam, a reluctant pagan seer, foresaw 'a star will come out of Jacob; a scepter will rise out of Israel,' a king who would crush God's enemies. Wise men from the east followed a star to Bethlehem to worship the newborn King, and Jesus closes Scripture calling Himself 'the bright Morning Star.'
Explanation: The oracle is striking because God spoke it through a hired prophet who came to curse Israel and could only bless. The star promises a royal deliverer rising from Jacob's line in God's timing, a promise the Magi's journey confirms and Revelation seals, as Christ's reign dawns over all nations.
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; The Birth of Jesus

Fulfillment: The ark, overlaid with gold and overshadowed by cherubim, carried the law, the manna, and Aaron's rod, and God's presence rested above it between the cherubim. In Christ, all that the ark held and signified comes together: He is God's presence with us, the law fulfilled, the true bread from heaven, and our resurrected High Priest.
Explanation: Israel carried the ark into battle, across the Jordan, and finally into the temple, confessing that the Lord Himself went before them. The ark pointed to a day when God would not merely go before His people in a box of gold-covered wood, but dwell with them in a person, Jesus Christ.
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Joshua; John; Romans; Hebrews; Revelation
RelatedEvents: Crossing the Jordan; Building of Solomon's Temple

Fulfillment: Alone in the wilderness, Jacob dreamed of a stairway reaching from earth to heaven, with angels ascending and descending, and God renewed the covenant promise above it. Jesus claimed that vision for Himself, telling Nathanael, 'You will see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.'
Explanation: Bethel, 'the house of God,' was an ordinary patch of ground until God revealed that heaven was nearer than Jacob knew. Jesus is the true ladder and the true Bethel: in Him, heaven and earth meet, God speaks His promises, and a runaway sinner finds the way home open.
RelatedEvents: Jacob Wrestles with God; The Birth of Jesus

Fulfillment: In Eden the tree of life stood at the garden's center, and after the fall its way was guarded so fallen humanity could not live forever in sin. At the cross, Jesus hung on a tree to bear the curse for us, and in the new Jerusalem the tree of life stands open again, its leaves for the healing of the nations.
Explanation: The Bible begins and ends around this tree, with exile in between, and Christ's cross, itself called a tree, stands at the turning point. What Adam lost by reaching for forbidden fruit, Jesus restores by His obedience, so all who wash their robes in His blood regain the right to eat and live.

Fulfillment: Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him from among Israel, putting God's words in his mouth, and that anyone who would not listen would be held accountable. Jesus is that prophet: He speaks only what the Father gives Him, He is authenticated by signs like Moses, and He mediates a new covenant. Peter preached this promise as fulfilled in Jesus, and Stephen repeated it before his martyrdom.
FulfillmentPassage: John 5:46; John 6:14; John 7:40; John 12:49; Acts 3:22-23; Acts 7:37; Hebrews 3:5-6
Explanation: Like Moses, Jesus speaks God's words directly (Deuteronomy 18:18; John 12:49), stands between God and the people, and is authenticated by signs. But Jesus is greater: Moses was a faithful servant in God's house, while Jesus is the Son over the house (Hebrews 3:5-6). The crowds recognized it themselves, saying after the feeding of the five thousand, "This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world" (John 6:14). See the Moses entry for the full set of parallels between their lives.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; The Feeding of the Five Thousand; Transfiguration

Fulfillment: When the tribes disputed the priesthood, each tribe's rod was laid up before the LORD, and only Aaron's rod budded, blossomed, and yielded almonds overnight — dead wood bringing forth life. It was kept in the ark as a sign against rebellion: life out of death, fruit from a dead stick, by God's choosing alone.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading, distinct from the Ark of the Covenant entry (which covers the chest, not its contents): the rod's overnight blossoming is a life-from-death sign, fulfilled in the One who is the resurrection and the life. Hebrews 9:4 confirms the rod was kept in the ark; the resurrection reading itself is traditional, stated as such.

Fulfillment: Abel offered the first acceptable sacrifice and became the first righteous sufferer, murdered by his own brother for doing right. His blood, Scripture says, cried out from the ground — and Hebrews sets that cry beside the blood of Jesus, which speaks a better word: not vengeance, but forgiveness.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading, anchored in Hebrews 12:24: Abel's blood speaks of a wrong that demands justice, while the blood of Jesus speaks of a wrong forgiven. The parallel is in the pattern — an innocent man slain, whose blood speaks after his death — not in Abel's life as a model. Abel offered in faith; Jesus is both the offering and the one who offers.

Fulfillment: When David's line looked cut down to a stump, the prophets promised a Branch from Jesse's roots — a righteous shoot who would grow up, build the temple, bear the glory, and sit and rule on His throne as priest and king at once. Paul quotes the Root of Jesse as the one in whom the Gentiles hope, and Revelation names Jesus the Root and the Offspring of David.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant for the figure: Romans 15:12 quotes Isaiah 11:10 ('the Root of Jesse') of Christ, and Revelation 22:16 names Him the Root and Offspring of David. The Branch and the Root of Jesse are the same Jesse-tree image, so they are one entry, not two; the temple-building and priest-king details come from Zechariah's Branch passages.
RelatedBooks: Isaiah; Jeremiah; Zechariah; Romans; Revelation; Luke
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; Jeremiah; Zechariah the Prophet; Jesus

Fulfillment: The Song sings of a bridegroom and his bride, and Hosea promises a betrothal that will last forever — 'I will betroth thee unto me for ever.' John the Baptist called himself the friend of the Bridegroom, and Paul says the marriage mystery is really about Christ and the church, consummated at the marriage supper of the Lamb.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading for the Song's bridegroom himself, with an explicit anchor for the pattern: Ephesians 5:32 says the marriage union is 'a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.' The Song is never quoted as a type in the New Testament, so the bridegroom identification is stated as traditional.
RelatedBooks: Song of Solomon; Hosea; John; Ephesians; Revelation

Fulfillment: On the eighth day every male child of Abraham's house was circumcised — the sign of the covenant cut into the flesh, marking a people set apart. Paul writes that in Christ believers are circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, in putting off the body of the flesh — the sign fulfilled when the flesh is cut away at the cross and in baptism.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: Colossians 2:11 names 'the circumcision of Christ' directly, tied to burial with Him in baptism, and Romans 2:29 locates true circumcision in the heart, by the Spirit. The rite pointed to a cutting away that only Christ's death accomplishes.

Fulfillment: When a leper was cleansed, the priest took two birds: one was slain over running water, and the other, dipped in its blood with cedar, scarlet, and hyssop, was released alive into the open field. One bird dies, one bird flies free — death and release in a single rite, performed for the outcast who could not enter the camp until he was clean.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the slain bird and the living bird carry the same twofold pattern as the two goats of the Day of Atonement — death borne and life set free — applied here to the cleansing of the untouchable. Jesus cleansed lepers and sent them to the priests with Moses' own rite, but the rite itself is never called a type in the New Testament, so this is stated as traditional. This is a specific rite, distinct from the general Sacrificial System entry.

Fulfillment: The stone the builders rejected became the head of the corner, and Isaiah promised a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation, laid in Zion. Jesus quoted the psalm against the leaders who rejected Him, and Peter applies both passages to Christ: the rejected stone is the foundation stone of God's house.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: Matthew 21:42 is Jesus quoting Psalm 118:22 of Himself, and 1 Peter 2:6-7 quotes Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:22 of Christ, while Ephesians 2:20 names Jesus Christ Himself the chief corner stone. This is distinct from the Rock in the Wilderness entry (water from the rock) and from the Stone Cut Without Hands entry (the kingdom stone).

Fulfillment: When the priests bearing the ark stepped into the Jordan in flood, the waters stood up in a heap, and all Israel crossed on dry ground into the promised land, raising twelve memorial stones from the riverbed. It is the second water-crossing: out of Egypt through the sea, and into rest through the river — a passage through waters of death into the land of promise.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the crossing pictures a passage through death into new life — buried and raised, as Paul describes baptism — and Hebrews notes that Joshua's entry did not itself give the final rest, which still remains. It is distinct from the Red Sea Crossing entry (out of slavery) because this crossing is into rest, not out of bondage.

Fulfillment: Cyrus, a pagan king who did not know God, was nevertheless called by name a century and a half before his birth, titled God's shepherd and His anointed, and used to end the exile and send God's people home to rebuild. He is the anointed deliverer who sets captives free by decree — a sketch, in a foreign king, of the Anointed One who sets captives free in truth.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Isaiah's use of 'anointed' for Cyrus is the Old Testament's own language, and Jesus opened His ministry by reading Isaiah's anointing passage as fulfilled in Himself. Cyrus is never called a type in the New Testament, so this is stated as traditional. Note: no Cyrus people profile exists yet, so RelatedPeople omits him rather than linking a name with no page.

Fulfillment: Daniel, thrown to the lions for praying to God, spent the night in a sealed stone den and came out alive in the morning, while his accusers were destroyed. The sealed stone, the night among the beasts, the morning deliverance, and the king's decree that followed all sketch the sealed tomb, the descent, and the resurrection morning.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the parallels are in the details — a stone sealed over the opening, an innocent man delivered from a place of death, enemies confounded, and a royal proclamation afterward. Daniel is never called a type in the New Testament, so the reading is stated as traditional, not explicit.

Fulfillment: Elijah, fed by ravens in a famine, raised a widow's only son, called down fire on Carmel, and was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind without dying. Jesus cited Elijah's ministry to a Gentile widow, stood with him glorified on the mountain, and, like him, left this world by ascent rather than by an ordinary death.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Elijah's career sketches the prophet who works wonders, confronts false gods, raises the dead, and is taken up. The parallels are real — the widow's son, the Gentile welcome, the mountain glory, the ascent — but the New Testament never calls Elijah a type, so this entry states the pattern as traditional, not explicit.

Fulfillment: Elisha, given a double portion of Elijah's spirit, multiplied a widow's oil, raised a dead boy, healed a Gentile leper, fed a hundred men from twenty loaves, and even after his own death a corpse thrown into his grave came back to life. His ministry reads like a rehearsal of the miracles of Jesus — provision, healing, raising the dead — down to the feeding of a multitude from too little bread.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Jesus Himself pointed to Naaman's healing when He spoke of a prophet unwelcome at home, and His answer to John's disciples — the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the dead are raised — matches Elisha's wonders point for point. Elisha is never called a type in the New Testament, so the reading is stated as traditional.

Fulfillment: Esther, a Jewish orphan raised to a throne, risked her life to approach the king uninvited — 'if I perish, I perish' — and by her intercession turned a decree of death into deliverance for her whole people. She is the mediator who stands between a death sentence and her people and pleads, at the risk of her own life, until it is reversed.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Esther's intercession sketches the one Mediator who stands between God and man and lays down His life for His friends. Esther herself is never called a type in the New Testament, so this is stated as traditional. Her story is told in full in 'Esther Saves Her People.'

Fulfillment: On the day after the sabbath in Passover week, Israel waved the first sheaf of the harvest before the LORD — the first and the best, offered while the rest of the harvest still stood in the fields. Paul names the fulfillment directly: Christ is risen from the dead and become the firstfruits of them that slept.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: 1 Corinthians 15:20 states it — 'now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.' The first sheaf guarantees the harvest that follows; the risen Christ guarantees the resurrection of His people. This is distinct from the Passover Lamb entry (the sacrifice) because Firstfruits is the resurrection offering.

Fulfillment: For seven days Israel lived in booths of branches, remembering the wilderness tents and rejoicing in the harvest — God dwelling with His people under open sky. John says the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us, and at this very feast Jesus stood and cried that whoever thirsts should come to Him for living water.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading, distinct from the Tabernacle entry (the tent structure): this is the feast of dwelling — booths, harvest joy, and the water-pouring rite that frames Jesus' living-water cry. John 1:14 uses the feast's own verb ('tabernacled'), and Revelation 21:3 carries the dwelling to its end, but the feast is never called a type in the New Testament, so this is stated as traditional.

Fulfillment: For seven days after Passover, Israel ate bread without leaven and cleared every trace of leaven from their houses — a week of clean bread for a people just delivered. Paul takes the feast up directly: Christ our passover is sacrificed for us, therefore let us keep the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant for the feast-connection (1 Corinthians 5:7-8 ties the feast to Christ's sacrifice); the further reading — leaven as sin, unleavened bread as Christ's sinlessness — is traditional and stated as such. This is distinct from the Passover Lamb entry (the lamb) because the bread is the feast's own element, kept for seven days.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Exodus and the Red Sea

Fulfillment: Israel is called God's firstborn son, set apart and claimed by God, and the firstborn of every house was redeemed by the lamb's blood. The New Testament takes the title and gives it to Jesus — firstborn of every creature, firstborn among many brethren, firstborn from the dead — the Son who inherits all things and brings many sons to glory.
Explanation: MIXED warrant, stated plainly: the title itself is explicitly applied to Christ in the New Testament (Colossians 1:15; Romans 8:29), while the reading of Israel-as-firstborn-son (Exodus 4:22) as a foreshadow of Christ the Son is traditional. This entry is distinct from the Passover Lamb entry, which covers the lamb that redeemed the firstborn, not the son-figure himself.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea

Fulfillment: David sang of the LORD as his shepherd, and Ezekiel promised that God Himself would shepherd His scattered flock and raise up one shepherd, His servant David, over them. Jesus claimed the office outright — 'I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep' — and Peter calls Him the chief Shepherd who appears with an unfading crown.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: John 10:11 is Jesus' own claim, and Hebrews 13:20 and 1 Peter 5:4 keep the shepherd titles for Him. This is distinct from the King David entry, which covers David's kingship; the shepherd office here is Ezekiel's promised shepherd, claimed by Jesus Himself.
RelatedBooks: Psalms; Ezekiel; Zechariah; John; Hebrews; 1 Peter

Fulfillment: Jeremiah, called before he was born to speak God's word to a people who would not listen, was mocked, beaten, and imprisoned for it, and wept over the city he could not save. Jesus, the prophet rejected by His own, wept over Jerusalem in almost the same words and was likewise rejected for telling the truth.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the 'weeping prophet' and the weeping Saviour stand in the same posture toward the same city, both sent to a people who would not be gathered. Jeremiah is never called a type in the New Testament, so this is stated as traditional.

Fulfillment: Job, blameless and upright, lost everything and still would not curse God; in the middle of his suffering he declared, 'I know that my redeemer liveth.' He is the righteous sufferer who intercedes for his friends and is restored double at the end — a sketch of the innocent one who suffers, prays for His tormentors, and is vindicated.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: James holds up 'the patience of Job' as the model of endurance, and Peter describes Christ suffering without retaliation, bearing our sins, by whose stripes we are healed. Job's redeemer confession points forward to a living Redeemer; Job himself is never called a type in the New Testament, so this is stated as traditional.

Fulfillment: When Joseph demanded Benjamin as a slave, Judah stepped forward and offered himself in his brother's place: let me bear the punishment so he can go free. It is the clearest picture in Genesis of substitution — one man volunteering to take another's sentence — and it points to the Substitute who takes ours.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Judah's offer is not called a type in the New Testament, but the shape matches exactly — a willing substitute, a guilty brother set free, a sentence transferred from the one who deserved it to the one who offered. Judah could only offer himself for one brother for a time; Jesus offers Himself for many, once and for all.
RelatedPeople: Judah; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Benjamin; Jesus

Fulfillment: Dying Jacob blessed Judah as a lion's whelp who crouches and rises, and said the scepter would not depart from Judah until tribute came to him. John, weeping because no one could open the sealed book, was told to stop weeping: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has prevailed to open it.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: Revelation 5:5 names the Lion of the tribe of Judah directly, and Hebrews 7:14 notes that our Lord sprang out of Judah. This entry covers the lion image only; the scepter-and-Shiloh oracle of Genesis 49:10 as a whole is treated in the report as a title-oracle and is not given a separate entry.

Fulfillment: Rahab was told to tie a scarlet cord in her window, and when Jericho fell, everyone in the house marked by the cord was spared. Scarlet is the color of blood, and the cord is the sign that turns a house of a condemned city into a house of salvation — the same logic as the blood on the doorposts, a visible sign that death passes over.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the cord's scarlet color and its function — a sign displayed in faith that spares a household from judgment — match the blood-signs of Passover, but the New Testament never calls the cord itself a type, so this is stated as traditional. Rahab herself is named in Hebrews 11 and in Jesus' genealogy.

Fulfillment: A red heifer without blemish, never yoked, was slain outside the camp and burned whole, and its ashes mixed with water purified anyone defiled by contact with death. It is the one sacrifice whose whole point is cleansing from death itself — and Hebrews notes that the bodies of such sacrifices were burned without the camp, as Jesus suffered without the gate.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading with a strong Hebrews anchor: Hebrews 13:11-13 draws the outside-the-camp parallel explicitly for the Day of Atonement sacrifices, and 9:13-14 reasons from ashes that purify the flesh to blood that purges the conscience. The red heifer itself is never named in the New Testament, so the identification is stated as traditional. This is a specific rite, distinct from the general Sacrificial System entry.

Fulfillment: Ruth, a Moabite widow with no claim on Israel, clung to Naomi, gleaned in a stranger's field, and was welcomed by Boaz the redeemer into the family and the line of David. She is the Gentile outsider brought near by grace alone — and she stands, by name, in the genealogy of Jesus.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Ruth's welcome pictures the welcome of the nations — those once far off, with no citizenship in Israel, brought near. Ruth is never called a type in the New Testament, so this is stated as traditional; it is distinct from the Boaz entry, which covers the redeemer rather than the one redeemed.

Fulfillment: God rested on the seventh day and made it holy, and Israel was commanded to keep it as a sign of creation and of deliverance from Egypt. Paul writes that sabbaths are a shadow of things to come, and Hebrews says a rest remains for the people of God — a rest entered by ceasing from one's own works, as God did from His.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: Colossians 2:17 calls sabbaths 'a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ,' and Hebrews 4:9-10 names the remaining rest. Jesus, Lord of the sabbath, is both the giver of the rest and the rest itself. This is distinct from the Year of Jubilee entry (a fiftieth-year release): the Sabbath is the weekly sign of rest.
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Exodus; Deuteronomy; Colossians; Hebrews; Mark

Fulfillment: Samson, blinded and bound, prayed for strength one last time and pulled down the pillars, killing more of Israel's enemies in his death than in his life. His death became his greatest victory — the pattern of a deliverer who defeats the enemy precisely by dying.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading, stated plainly: Samson's life is no model — it is marked by compromise and failure — but the shape of his end points to the cross. Through death, Hebrews says, Jesus destroyed him who had the power of death; at the cross, Paul says, He disarmed the powers and triumphed over them. The parallel is in the death-victory, not in Samson's character.

Fulfillment: God promised Abraham that in his seed all the nations of the earth would be blessed — a promise repeated at the very mountain where Abraham offered his son and received him back. Paul insists the promise was spoken to a seed, singular, and that seed is Christ: the one descendant through whom the blessing reaches every nation.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: Galatians 3:16 states it directly — 'he saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ.' This is distinct from the seed of Genesis 3:15 (covered in the Adam entry): that is the woman's seed promised at the Fall; this is Abraham's seed promised at Moriah.

Fulfillment: Solomon, son of David, reigned in peace, built the house of God, and was given wisdom wider than any king before him, so that rulers came from afar to hear him. Jesus Himself said that one greater than Solomon is here — greater in wisdom, greater in peace, and the true builder of God's house.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading, distinct from the Solomon's Temple entry (which covers the building): Solomon the person foreshadows Christ the King — son of David, prince of peace, possessor of wisdom, builder of the house. Where Solomon's wisdom was a gift and his peace was bounded by his lifetime, Jesus is wisdom itself and His peace has no end.

Fulfillment: Daniel saw one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, brought before the Ancient of Days, and given dominion, glory, and a kingdom that all peoples would serve and that would never be destroyed. Jesus took this figure as His own name for Himself more than any other, and before the council He declared that they would see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: Jesus Himself applies Daniel's figure to Himself, and the New Testament keeps the title — in the Gospels, in Stephen's vision, and in Revelation's description of one like a son of man among the lampstands. This is not a traditional reading but the New Testament's own identification.

Fulfillment: Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and clay, until a stone cut out without hands struck the image, shattered it, and grew into a great mountain that filled the whole earth. Daniel explained it as a kingdom God Himself would set up, which would break every human empire and stand forever.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading, distinct from the Cornerstone entry (a foundation stone) and the Rock in the Wilderness (water from a rock): this stone is a kingdom, not a building — cut without human hands, crushing the empires, growing until it fills the earth. Jesus' own stone sayings in Matthew 21:44 and Luke 20:18 give the application its anchor, but Daniel 2 is never quoted as a type in the New Testament, so this is stated as traditional.

Fulfillment: Isaiah sang of a vineyard planted by God that yielded only wild grapes, and the psalmist recalled a vine brought out of Egypt that spread across the land and was then broken down. Israel was the vine that failed — so Jesus declares Himself the vine that does not fail: 'I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.'
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: John 15:1 is Jesus' own claim, set against Isaiah's failed vineyard and the psalm's broken vine. This is distinct from the Tree of Life entry (Eden's tree and the cross): the vine is Israel's covenant plant, replaced by a true vine whose branches bear fruit by abiding.

Fulfillment: Israel, tested forty years in the wilderness, failed at every turn — grumbling for bread, water, and gods they could see. Jesus, tested forty days in the same wilderness, answered every temptation from Deuteronomy and did not fail once. Where the old people broke, the new head of the people held.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: 1 Corinthians 10:6 says these things 'were our examples' — the Greek word is typoi, types — and Paul lists the cloud, the sea, the manna, and the rock as written for our admonition. The parts (Red Sea, Manna, Rock) already have entries; this entry covers the testing pattern itself, which has none: forty years of failure set against forty days of victory.

Fulfillment: Zerubbabel, governor of the returned exiles and descendant of David, laid the foundation of the second temple when the work seemed hopeless, and God called him His signet ring — the chosen seal of His authority. He stands in the genealogy of Jesus, the governor who rebuilds what was ruined and the signet by which God seals His work.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Zerubbabel's two roles — Davidic governor and temple-builder — both land on Christ, who is of David's line and who builds the true temple, His own body raised in three days. The signet-ring promise is never applied to Jesus in the New Testament, so this is stated as traditional.

Fulfillment: Noah, the righteous man who found grace and was saved through the waters of judgment, prefigures Christ, through whom a new humanity is saved through the waters of baptism and the judgment of the cross. As Noah's ark carried his household safely through the flood, so Christ carries His people safely through death into new life.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Noah is the righteous head of a new humanity after judgment — the man through whom God preserves a remnant and begins again. The New Testament explicitly connects the flood and the ark with baptism (1 Peter 3:20-21) and commends Noah's faith (Hebrews 11:7); the person-typology is the traditional reading built on that explicit link. Noah is called a preacher of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5), and like Christ he stands between a condemned world and the family God saves.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood; Baptism of Jesus; Crucifixion of Jesus; Resurrection of Jesus

Fulfillment: Isaac, the beloved only son of promise, who carried the wood for his own sacrifice up Mount Moriah and was received back as from the dead, prefigures Jesus, the beloved Son given by the Father, who carried His cross and rose again.
Explanation: Abraham offered his only son Isaac on Mount Moriah, and Isaac carried the wood for the offering (Genesis 22:6) as Jesus carried His cross. Hebrews says Abraham received Isaac back 'in a figure' of resurrection (Hebrews 11:19), and Paul calls believers children of promise 'like Isaac' (Galatians 4:28). Isaac is the son of promise and heir through whom the covenant line runs.
RelatedEvents: Birth of Isaac; The Binding of Isaac; Crucifixion of Jesus; Resurrection of Jesus

Fulfillment: As Gideon defeated Midian not with an army but with three hundred men carrying trumpets, pitchers, and torches — so that Israel could not boast in its own strength — Jesus wins His victory through what the world counts as weakness: a cross, and a small band of witnesses. Isaiah ties the breaking of Midian's yoke to the coming Child whose government will have no end.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Gideon is never called a type in the New Testament, but the shape matches — God raises a deliverer, strips away human strength so the victory is plainly the LORD's (Judges 7:2), and breaks the oppressor's yoke, the very image Isaiah 9:4 uses for the Messiah's work. Gideon first tears down Baal's altar, builds an altar called 'The LORD Is Peace,' and then delivers a people who could not deliver themselves.

Fulfillment: Samuel served the LORD as prophet, priest, and judge, and never ceased interceding for Israel. Jesus holds all three offices perfectly — Prophet who speaks God's word, Priest who offers Himself, and King who judges justly — and He ever lives to intercede for His people.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Samuel is never called a type in the New Testament, but the correspondences are close: a child given in answer to prayer and lent to the LORD, who 'grew on, and was in favour both with the LORD, and also with men' (1 Samuel 2:26) — the very pattern Luke 2:52 uses for Jesus — and who combined the work of prophet, priest, and judge while interceding for a sinful people (1 Samuel 12:23).
RelatedEvents: Calling of Samuel; Samuel - Last Judge and Prophet; David Anointed by Samuel

Fulfillment: Hezekiah trusted the LORD when Assyria threatened, prayed as Jerusalem was surrounded, and was delivered from a sickness unto death — his life extended and his tears seen. Jesus is the King who trusts perfectly, bears the siege of sin and death itself, and rises, His life not merely extended but endless.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Hezekiah is never called a type in the New Testament, but the shape matches — a king who 'trusted in the LORD God of Israel' (2 Kings 18:5), cleansed the house of God, prayed when death and an army stood at the gate, and was heard: 'I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears' (Isaiah 38:5). His recovery from sickness unto death pictures, in a lesser key, the King who passes through death and comes out alive.
RelatedEvents: Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion; Hezekiah, Josiah, and Judah's Reforms

Fulfillment: Ezra prepared his heart to seek the Law, to do it, and to teach it; he led exiles home from captivity and stood between a sinful people and God in prayer. Jesus is the Teacher who fulfills the Law He teaches, leads His people out of a deeper captivity, and ever intercedes for them.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Ezra is never called a type in the New Testament, but the pattern is close — priest and 'ready scribe in the law of Moses' (Ezra 7:6) who sought, did, and taught the Law (Ezra 7:10), brought the captives home, and confessed the people's sin as his own (Ezra 9:6). The scribe who teaches with authority and the priest who intercedes meet in Christ, who is both.

Fulfillment: Nehemiah left the king's court when he heard Jerusalem lay in ruins, wept and prayed for his people, and rebuilt the wall in fifty-two days against mockery and threat — then cleansed God's house of what defiled it. Jesus left His Father's glory for a ruined people, wept over Jerusalem, finished His work against every opposition, and cleanses the temple of His people.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Nehemiah is never called a type in the New Testament, but the shape matches — the king's cupbearer who gives up comfort for a broken city, intercedes with fasting and confession (Nehemiah 1:4-11), rallies the people with 'the God of heaven, he will prosper us' (Nehemiah 2:20), completes the wall despite Sanballat's threats, and casts the defiling goods out of the temple chambers (Nehemiah 13:8), as Jesus would cleanse the temple in His day.

Fulfillment: Ezekiel was commanded to lie on his side and bear the iniquity of Israel and Judah as a living sign, and God twice calls him a sign to the people. Jesus does not merely picture bearing sin but truly bears it: He was made sin for us, bore our sins in His own body on the tree, and was once offered to bear the sins of many. As watchman, Ezekiel warned of judgment to come; Christ warns and rescues.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Ezekiel's sign-acts — bearing the people's iniquity on his side for 390 and 40 days, and standing before the exiles as a sign — correspond to Christ, who truly bears the sins of His people rather than picturing it. His watchman office, warning the people of judgment, echoes Christ, who warns and rescues. The New Testament never calls Ezekiel a type, so this is stated as traditional.
RelatedEvents: Ezekiel's Call; Ezekiel's Sign-Acts of the Siege; Ezekiel and Daniel in Exile

Fulfillment: Jacob's life — exile and return, wrestling and blessing, the father of the twelve tribes — is sometimes read as a shadow of Christ, who leaves His Father's house, wrestles for His people, and gathers the twelvefold people of God.
Explanation: DOUBT: no single passage or act of Jacob maps cleanly onto Christ; the parallels are diffuse. The ladder at Bethel is already covered by the live 'Jacob's Ladder' entry; the crossed-hands blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh (Genesis 48) is sometimes read as a cross-shape, but that is a visual resemblance rather than a stated correspondence; and the 'man' Jacob wrestled (Genesis 32) is an appearance of God, not a Jacob-type. TRADITIONAL reading: at most, Jacob the chosen younger son and father of Israel shadows Christ as head of the true Israel — but the case is suggestive, not strong.
RelatedEvents: Jacob's Ladder at Bethel; Jacob Wrestles with God at Peniel; Jacob's Return and Reconciliation

Fulfillment: Enoch, who walked with God and was taken without seeing death, faintly prefigures Christ's ascension — the man who passes from earthly life into God's presence alive.
Explanation: DOUBT: the correspondence is a single point — translation without death — with no broader life-parallel; Enoch's story is four verses long. TRADITIONAL reading: Enoch's being taken (Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5) is sometimes read as a shadow of Christ's ascension (Acts 1:9), but the New Testament never draws that parallel; Hebrews commends Enoch's faith, not a typology.

Fulfillment: Benjamin, the 'son of the right hand,' born in sorrow and renamed in favor, is sometimes read as a faint shadow of Christ, the Son at the Father's right hand who was born to sorrow and raised to honor.
Explanation: DOUBT: the parallel rests almost entirely on the meaning of the name ('son of the right hand') plus a birth-in-sorrow motif; Benjamin's own life — favored youngest brother, the cup in his sack — has no act that maps onto Christ's work, and the substitution in Genesis 44 is Judah's type, already covered by the live 'Judah' entry. TRADITIONAL reading: at most a name-based hint toward Christ seated at the right hand (Hebrews 1:3).
RelatedPeople: Benjamin; Jacob; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Judah; Jesus

Fulfillment: Aaron, the first high priest, who bore the names of Israel on his breastplate and made atonement once a year, prefigures Christ, the great High Priest who bears His people before God and made atonement once for all.
Explanation: DOUBT: this entry substantially overlaps the live 'The High Priest' entry, which already covers the office, and Aaron's personal record breaks the parallel — he made the golden calf (Exodus 32) and was barred with Moses from the land (Numbers 20:12). TRADITIONAL reading: Aaron's priestly mediation — bearing names over his heart (Exodus 28:29) and entering the holy place with blood (Leviticus 16) — shadows Christ's perpetual intercession (Hebrews 7:25; Hebrews 9:11-12), but the office, not Aaron's life, carries the type.
RelatedEvents: The Consecration of Aaron and His Sons; The Golden Calf; The Deaths of Miriam and Aaron; Crucifixion of Jesus

Fulfillment: Bezaleel, filled with the Spirit of God to build the tabernacle, God's dwelling among His people, faintly prefigures Christ, who builds the true temple — His body and His church — as God's dwelling among us.
Explanation: DOUBT: the correspondence is a single point — a Spirit-filled builder of God's dwelling — and Bezaleel's work is already covered in substance by the live 'Tabernacle' entry. TRADITIONAL reading: the Spirit's endowment for building (Exodus 31:3) is sometimes linked to Christ the builder (Matthew 16:18; John 2:19-21), but the New Testament never draws that parallel.

Fulfillment: Caleb, who followed the Lord fully when the majority feared, and who at eighty-five still claimed the promised inheritance, faintly prefigures Christ, the faithful witness who trusts the Father's promise and leads God's people into their inheritance.
Explanation: DOUBT: the parallel is generic faithfulness — any faithful believer parallels it — with no act of Caleb's that distinctively maps onto Christ's person or work; Caleb is a model of perseverance, and Joshua (already a live entry) carries the leader-into-the-land typology. TRADITIONAL reading: Caleb's 'different spirit' (Numbers 14:24) and his wholehearted following are sometimes read as a shadow of Christ's perfect trust, but the case is suggestive, not strong.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies; Wilderness Wanderings; Crossing the Jordan

Fulfillment: Deborah judged Israel and sent Barak into battle against Sisera, and the victory song celebrates the LORD who routed the enemy. If she pictures Christ at all, it is only in the general office of judge and deliverer — every judge delivered Israel, and nothing in her story maps to His priestly or atoning work.
Explanation: BORDERLINE — doubt: Deborah's deliverance of Israel is genuine, but the judge-pattern is generic — Othniel, Ehud, and Gideon all delivered Israel too — and her story offers no specific correspondence to Christ's person or work beyond 'a leader who won a battle.' Her prophetic office does not map to Christ's offices in any particular way. TRADITIONAL reading (doubtful): a judge raised up to save a people who cried out.

Fulfillment: Jonathan loved David as his own soul, stripped off his robe and gave it with his sword and bow, pleaded for David's life before Saul, and yielded his own claim to the throne. If he pictures Christ at all, it is in self-emptying covenant love — but Jonathan dies without delivering anyone, and the love runs toward David the king rather than from the King to His people.
Explanation: BORDERLINE — doubt: Jonathan's covenant love is beautiful, but the direction of the picture runs the wrong way for a type of Christ: Jonathan is the friend who gives everything to David, whereas Christ is the King who gives everything for His friends. He lays down no life for David's sake in any atoning sense, and his story ends in death on Mount Gilboa, not deliverance. TRADITIONAL reading (doubtful): the prince who surrendered his throne-right to the anointed king.
RelatedPeople: Jonathan, Son of Saul; King David; Jesus

Fulfillment: When Abiathar sided with Adonijah, Zadok stayed loyal to David, anointed Solomon, and took the priesthood the LORD had promised to 'a faithful priest.' If he pictures Christ at all, it is in the faithful-priest office — but Zadok's story is mostly loyalty to a king, and his priestly work itself is barely narrated.
Explanation: BORDERLINE — doubt: the faithful-priest correspondence is real in outline — 1 Samuel 2:35 promises a priest who 'shall walk before mine anointed for ever,' and Zadok fills that seat — but Zadok's own narrative is that of a loyal supporter, not a priest whose ministry prefigures Christ's sacrifice or intercession in any detail. The office maps; the story barely does. TRADITIONAL reading (doubtful): the priest who stayed faithful when the other priest chose the usurper.
RelatedPeople: Zadok, High Priest; King David; King Solomon; Jesus
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; Solomon and the First Temple

Fulfillment: Josiah tore his clothes at the rediscovered Law, renewed the covenant, purged the idols, and kept a Passover like none since Samuel's day — then died young at Megiddo. If he pictures Christ at all, it is in the reforming king who restores God's word and keeps the feast — but his death does not atone, and every reforming king cleansed the land.
Explanation: BORDERLINE — doubt: Josiah's reform is the fullest in Kings, but 'a good king who restored worship' is the generic pattern of Asa, Jehoshaphat, and Hezekiah, and Josiah adds no distinctive correspondence to Christ's person or work — his Passover keeps the feast, it does not become it, and his death at Megiddo is a political disaster, not a sacrifice. TRADITIONAL reading (doubtful): the boy-king whose heart was tender at the word of God.
RelatedEvents: Josiah's Reforms and the Book of the Law

Fulfillment: Jehoiada hid the child-king Joash from Athaliah's slaughter, crowned him in the temple, made a covenant between the LORD and the king and people, and restored true worship. If he pictures Christ at all, it is in the priest who preserves the promised king — but Jehoiada serves the king; he is not the king, and his priesthood guards a throne rather than atoning for a people.
Explanation: BORDERLINE — doubt: the hidden-child-king pattern is genuinely suggestive — a priest shelters the rightful heir from a usurper who murders the royal seed, then crowns him — but the parallel centers on Joash, not Jehoiada: Jehoiada is the protector, and protectors (like the nurse in 2 Kings 11:2, or Joseph in Matthew 2) are guardians of the type, not the type itself. Joash himself is already drafted in round 2. TRADITIONAL reading (doubtful): the priest who kept the lamp of David alive.
RelatedPeople: Jehoiada, High Priest; Joash, King of Judah; Athaliah; Jesus

Fulfillment: The blessed man of Psalm 1 delights in the law of the LORD and meditates on it day and night, standing like a tree planted by streams of water, fruitful in season and unwithering. Jesus is the only man who perfectly delighted in God's law and did His Father's will, the one who fulfills the Law rather than merely keeping it, and in whom believers abide and bear fruit.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the blessed man is read as a portrait of Christ, the perfectly righteous man who delights in the law, prospers like the tree by the water, and stands when the ungodly are driven away like chaff. DOUBT: the figure is an unnamed, generic wisdom ideal, not an individual person with a life, office, or action of his own; the correspondence rests on ideal righteousness rather than a specific narrative parallel, and Psalm 1 functions as a wisdom prologue to the Psalter rather than a personal history. This may be wisdom portraiture rather than a true type, so it is held as borderline, not clear.

Fulfillment: The voice that cries, 'Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow,' has long been heard at the cross, where passers-by reviled a suffering Saviour; and the same voice that remembers affliction still hopes in mercies new every morning. Jesus is the truly afflicted man, acquainted with grief, who yet trusted the Father through it.
Explanation: BORDERLINE: TRADITIONAL reading — Christian hymnody and devotion have long applied Lamentations 1:12 to Christ on the cross, and Lamentations 3's movement from affliction to hope in mercy echoes His trust in suffering. The doubt: the speaker is not a named individual but a poetic voice — Jeremiah, or Jerusalem personified — so this is a voice applied to Christ, not a person whose life prefigures Him. Held as borderline for that reason.
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah and the Fall of Jerusalem

Fulfillment: Amos, a herdsman taken from following the flock, interceded for Israel until judgment was turned aside, and was rejected by Amaziah the priest for speaking God's word. Jesus, taken from lowly obscurity, ever lives to intercede for His people and was rejected by the chief priests for telling the truth.
Explanation: BORDERLINE: TRADITIONAL reading — the parallels are real: a lowly call, intercession that turns away judgment, rejection by the religious establishment. The doubt: each element is common to the prophets — Moses and Jeremiah both interceded and were rejected — and no passage of Scripture connects Amos with Christ. The correspondence is a shared prophetic pattern rather than a distinctive type, so this entry is held as borderline.

Fulfillment: God told Hosea to marry an unfaithful wife, and then, after she had left him, to love her again and buy her back — paying the price to redeem the wife who had sold herself away. It is the story of a husband who will not let an unfaithful bride go, and it points to the Bridegroom who pays to redeem an unfaithful people and make them His own.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Hosea is never called a type in the New Testament, but the shape matches — a husband redeeming an unfaithful bride at his own cost, set beside Paul's picture of Christ loving the church and giving Himself for her. Hosea's wife stands for unfaithful Israel; the church, not Christ, is the bride in the fulfillment. Hosea's own marriage is the picture, not the person redeemed.

Fulfillment: Mordecai refused to bow to Haman, mourned for his people under the death decree, and was then honored by the very man who meant to hang him — paraded in royal robes on the king's horse — before being raised to second place in the kingdom. The humbled man is exalted, and his exaltation becomes his people's deliverance.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the humiliation-to-exaltation pattern matches Philippians 2, where Christ humbled Himself and God highly exalted Him — but Mordecai is never called a type in the New Testament, so this is stated as traditional. Mordecai's exaltation serves his people's rescue; it does not atone. Esther's own intercession is a separate entry.

Fulfillment: Naboth would not sell his ancestral vineyard, so Jezebel had false witnesses swear against him, and he was stoned to death outside the city so the king could seize his vineyard. An innocent man, condemned by false testimony, killed outside the walls so another could take what was his.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: no New Testament writer calls Naboth a type, but three details converge — false witnesses, death outside the city, and a vineyard seized by killing the rightful heir, matching the vineyard parable where the tenants kill the son to seize the inheritance. Naboth's death did not atone; the parallel is in the pattern of innocent suffering, not in the efficacy.
RelatedPeople: Naboth the Jezreelite; King Ahab; Jezebel; Jesus

Fulfillment: When Israel's sin brought a plague on the camp, Phinehas the priest acted with zeal, and the plague stopped. God said he had turned away His wrath, and gave him a covenant of peace and an everlasting priesthood — wrath averted by a priest's act, and a priesthood that would not end.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Phinehas is never called a type in the New Testament, but the shape is there — zeal for God's honor (echoed in Jesus cleansing the temple), wrath turned away by a priestly act, and an everlasting priesthood, which Hebrews assigns to Christ alone. Phinehas's act stopped a plague for a generation; Christ's priesthood is unchangeable and His atonement is once for all.
RelatedPeople: Phinehas; Zimri, Son of Salu; Cozbi; Jesus

Fulfillment: When Athaliah seized the throne and murdered the royal seed, the infant Joash was hidden in the temple for six years, kept alive in secret while a usurper reigned — then brought out, crowned, and acclaimed king, and a covenant was made between the LORD, the king, and the people.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the preserved royal child hidden from a murderous ruler matches the infancy pattern — a king's seed kept alive in secret and then revealed — but no New Testament writer calls Joash a type, so this is stated as traditional. Joash's reign later failed when his protector died; the pattern is in the preservation and revealing, not in Joash's whole life.
RelatedPeople: Joash, King of Judah; Jehosheba, Daughter of Jehoram; Athaliah; Jesus

Fulfillment: Joshua stood before the LORD in filthy garments, accused by Satan, and was stripped of the filth, clothed in clean garments, and given a clean turban — then crowned, with the word that he would be a priest upon his throne, a sign of the Branch to come.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Zechariah calls Joshua and his fellows 'men wondered at' — signs pointing to the Branch — and the crowned priest upon a throne is the priest-king picture Hebrews assigns to Christ. Joshua himself is not the Branch; he is the sign of Him. This entry is distinct from The Branch entry (the figure) and from Joshua the conqueror (a separate person and entry).
RelatedPeople: Joshua, Son of Jehozadak; Zechariah the Prophet; Jesus

Fulfillment: Elihu told Job that if there is a messenger with a sufferer, an interpreter, one among a thousand, to show him what is right — then God is gracious, and says, 'Deliver him from going down to the pit: I have found a ransom.' A mediator who declares what is right, and a ransom found, so the sufferer need not die.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Elihu's words are the Old Testament's clearest picture of a mediator and a ransom together, and Paul names Christ as the one mediator who gave Himself a ransom for all. Elihu himself is not called a type in the New Testament, and he is a young friend speaking in a debate, not a redeemer — the parallel is in his words about mediation and ransom, not in his person as a whole.

Fulfillment: After Elisha died and was buried, a dead man cast hastily into his grave touched the prophet's bones and came back to life, standing on his feet. Life came through contact with the dead — from a grave, unexpectedly, to a man who had no hope of it.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading, stated as such: a single verse with no New Testament citation, offered as a pattern parallel only — life through contact with death, matching the claim that believers are planted together with Christ in the likeness of His death and raised in the likeness of His resurrection. The bones are not a redeemer; the parallel is in the mechanism, life from death.

Fulfillment: After the first sin, Adam and Eve covered themselves with fig leaves, and God replaced their covering with coats of skins — a covering that cost a life, made by God Himself, to clothe the guilty. The first sacrifice in Scripture is not offered by man, but provided by God.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: Genesis does not say an animal was sacrificed, and no New Testament writer calls the coats a type — but the shape is the classic one: man's own covering replaced by a God-provided covering that required death, matching the call to be clothed with Christ and with garments of salvation. The parallel is in the covering, not in any stated sacrifice.

Fulfillment: God told Abraham to cut animals in two and lay the pieces opposite each other, as parties to a covenant would walk between them — but a deep sleep fell on Abraham, and only God passed between the pieces, as a smoking furnace and a burning lamp. God alone walked the path of the curse, taking both sides of the covenant upon Himself.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the rite itself is not called a type in the New Testament, but the shape matches — the covenant curse falling on God alone, and Paul's claim that Christ bore the curse of the law, with Hebrews' note that God swore by Himself because He could swear by no greater. The smoking furnace and burning lamp are God's presence in the rite, not a separate Christophany entry.

Fulfillment: Wisdom speaks as one possessed by the LORD from the beginning, before His works of old — present when He prepared the heavens, rejoicing before Him, delighting in the sons of men — and builds her house and prepares her feast, calling all who will come.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading, with a strong New Testament echo: Paul calls Christ 'the wisdom of God' and says He is made unto us wisdom, and Colossians hides all treasures of wisdom in Him — but no New Testament writer explicitly identifies Proverbs 8's figure as Christ, so this is stated as traditional, not explicit. Honest note: Proverbs 8:22's wording ('possessed' vs 'created') has been debated since the early church; the entry rests on the figure's role at creation, not on settling that verse.

Fulfillment: In that day, Zechariah says, a fountain shall be opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem for sin and for uncleanness — a source of cleansing that does not run dry, opened for the very people who need it.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the fountain's cleansing from sin matches the blood and water from Christ's pierced side and John's claim that His blood cleanses from all sin, but Zechariah's fountain is not called a type in the New Testament, so this is stated as traditional. It is distinct from the Bronze Laver entry (priestly washing): the fountain is the opened source of cleansing from sin itself.

Fulfillment: God took the key of the house of David from an unfaithful steward and laid it on Eliakim's shoulder: he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open. The key is authority over the house — who comes in, and who does not.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading, with a direct New Testament echo: Revelation gives the key of David to Christ Himself, who opens and no man shuts. The type is carried by the key, not by Eliakim — he was a flawed steward whose own peg was later removed (Isaiah 22:25), so he is named in the entry but not made the type.

Fulfillment: If a servant, offered his freedom, says, 'I love my master... I will not go out free,' his master brings him to the doorpost and bores his ear with an awl, and he serves forever — not driven, but willing, marked by love.
Explanation: SPLIT warrant: the willing-servant words are explicit — Psalm 40's 'mine ears hast thou opened... I delight to do thy will' is applied to Christ in Hebrews 10 — but the link from that psalm back to the bored-ear law of Exodus 21 is traditional inference, stated as such. The servant's mark is love, not coercion; Christ took the servant's form willingly.

Type: Release at the High Priest's Death
Fulfillment: A man who killed unintentionally fled to a city of refuge and stayed there — until the death of the high priest. After the high priest's death, the slayer could return home free. Freedom came, by law, only through the high priest's death.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the mechanism — release through the high priest's death — matches the claim that death frees from sin and that Christ's death redeems from transgressions, but no New Testament writer cites Numbers 35 as a type, so this is stated as traditional. It is distinct from the Cities of Refuge entry (the refuge itself): this entry is the release mechanism, the death that sets free.

Type: The Marriage of Adam and Eve
Fulfillment: God formed Eve from Adam's side and joined them as one flesh, the first marriage — and Paul quotes that very union as the pattern of Christ and the church: 'This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.'
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: Ephesians 5:31 quotes Genesis 2:24 ('they two shall be one flesh') and verse 32 applies it directly to Christ and the church. The first marriage is therefore not merely an illustration Paul borrows but a union whose one-flesh pattern finds its full meaning in Christ's union with His people. This entry is distinct from the live Bridegroom entry (the Song/Hosea bridegroom figure): this is the Genesis institution of marriage itself.

Fulfillment: Paul reads the two women of Abraham's household as two covenants: Hagar the bondwoman, whose son was born after the flesh, answers to Mount Sinai and bondage, while Sarah the freewoman, whose son was born by promise, answers to the Jerusalem above, which is free and is the mother of us all. Believers are children of promise, like Isaac, free in Christ.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: Galatians 4:24 states it — 'which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants.' The parallel is covenantal rather than personal: neither woman is herself Christ, but Sarah's promised son and the freedom of her household point to the new covenant in Christ, set against the bondage of law-keeping. This entry is distinct from the live Seed of Abraham entry (the promised seed as Christ): this is the two-women allegory of the two covenants.

Fulfillment: Once a year the high priest alone entered the Holy of Holies with blood, first for himself and then for the people, to make atonement for the sins of the whole nation. Hebrews presents Christ as the high priest who entered once for all, not with the blood of goats and calves but with His own blood, into the true Holy Place, having obtained eternal redemption.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: Hebrews 9 draws the parallel directly, contrasting the yearly entrance with blood not his own against Christ's single entrance with His own blood, and the repeated sacrifices against His once-for-all offering. This entry is distinct from its parts, which already have entries: the Mercy Seat (the object sprinkled), the Scapegoat (the goat sent away), and the Sacrificial System (the system in general). This entry covers the day as a whole — the yearly entrance pattern that Hebrews says Christ fulfills by entering heaven itself for us.

Fulfillment: Fifty days after the first sheaf was waved, Israel kept the Feast of Weeks: a harvest feast with two wave loaves, a freewill offering, and a command to leave gleanings for the poor and the stranger. On that very feast day in Jerusalem, the Spirit fell, the apostles preached in many tongues, and three thousand souls were added — the firstfruits of a worldwide harvest.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the New Testament never calls the Feast of Weeks a type, but the fulfillment lands on the feast's own day — Pentecost is the Greek name for Weeks — and the harvest pattern fits: Firstfruits (already a live entry, Christ risen) is followed fifty days later by a gathered harvest, now the church. The two loaves, offered with leaven unlike any other offering, are traditionally read as Jew and Gentile gathered into one harvest. This entry is distinct from the Feast of Firstfruits entry (the sheaf, Christ's resurrection): this is the fiftieth-day harvest feast.

Type: The Man Hanged on a Tree
Fulfillment: The law commanded that a man executed for a capital crime and hanged on a tree must not remain overnight, 'for he that is hanged is accursed of God.' Paul applies that curse directly to Christ: He redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, 'for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.'
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: Galatians 3:13 quotes Deuteronomy 21:23 of Christ's crucifixion. The parallel is in the curse-bearing, not in the criminal: Christ was no lawbreaker, but He bore the law's curse on a tree so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles. This entry is distinct from the live Sacrificial System entry (offerings in general): this is the specific tree-curse provision and Paul's explicit application of it.

Fulfillment: One champion fights in place of the whole army, and his victory becomes his people's victory: the shepherd boy faces the giant in the LORD's name, fells him with a stone from a sling, and the Philistine army flees. So Jesus fights as our representative champion, destroying the devil and death in His own death and resurrection, that His people may share His victory.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: this row is the single battle, not the man — David himself is already covered by the live 'King David' entry, which does not cite 1 Samuel 17. The representative shape is the point: Goliath demands a champion to decide the fate of both sides (1 Samuel 17:8-10, 16), Israel is dismayed, and one man stands in their place.
