The New Testament never calls this battle a type, so the parallel is stated as traditional.

Type: The Altar on Araunah's Threshing Floor
Fulfillment: When plague falls on Israel for David's census, the LORD stays the destroying angel at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, and David insists on paying the full price, refusing an offering that costs him nothing. The altar he builds there becomes the site of Solomon's temple. In Christ, the costly sacrifice that turns away wrath and the temple where God meets His people are one.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the pattern is a sacrifice, paid for at full price (2 Samuel 24:24), that stops a plague, on ground that then becomes the temple site (2 Chronicles 3:1, Mount Moriah). It is distinct from the live 'Solomon's Temple' entry, which covers the building: this row covers the atoning altar that precedes it. The New Testament never names Araunah's altar a type, so the reading is stated as traditional.
RelatedBooks: 2 Samuel; 1 Chronicles; 2 Chronicles; Romans; John; Hebrews
RelatedPeople: King David; Araunah the Jebusite; Jesus

Fulfillment: The elders who hated and expelled Jephthah return to beg him to be their head and captain, and the Spirit-empowered outcast delivers Israel from Ammon. So the stone the builders rejected becomes the head of the corner: Jesus, rejected by His own, becomes head and deliverer of His people.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the parallel is in rejection and exaltation only — 'Did not ye hate me, and expel me out of my father's house?' (Judges 11:7), answered by 'be our head' (Judges 11:8-11). It is NOT in his rash vow (Judges 11:30-40), which this entry does not commend and deliberately does not cite as its passage. The New Testament never names Jephthah a type, so the reading is stated as traditional.

Fulfillment: David seeks out a lame, hidden grandson of his enemy Saul — not to punish him but to show him 'the kindness of God' for Jonathan's sake, restoring his grandfather's land and seating him at the king's table continually. So God seeks out the undeserving, restores what was lost, and seats the lame and the outcast at His own table by grace alone.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: the pattern is the king's seeking kindness to one who cannot walk to him and has no claim — Mephibosheth hides in Lo-debar and calls himself a 'dead dog' (2 Samuel 9:8), and eats at the king's table 'continually' (2 Samuel 9:13). This is the recipient side of grace, distinct from the live 'King David' entry which covers David himself, and parallel to the live 'Ruth' entry, which likewise covers the one welcomed rather than the redeemer.
RelatedPeople: Mephibosheth, Son of Jonathan; King David; Jonathan; Jesus

Fulfillment: Psalm 68 sings of God ascending on high in triumphal procession, leading captivity captive and receiving gifts among men, His goings seen in the sanctuary. Paul quotes the ascent verse directly of Christ: when He ascended up on high He led captivity captive and gave gifts unto men, the same One who first descended and then ascended far above all heavens.
Explanation: EXPLICIT warrant: Ephesians 4:8 quotes Psalm 68:18 and applies it to Christ's ascension, so this is Scripture's own parallel, not an imposed one. The pattern is a victor's ascent after triumph, with captives led in train and gifts distributed — the shape of the ascension after the victory of the cross and resurrection. Honest note: the psalm says the ascender 'received gifts for men' while Ephesians says He 'gave gifts unto men'; Paul reads the ascended victor as the giver, and the entry rests on the ascent, captives, and gifts together, not on smoothing over that change of direction. No live or round-2 entry covers the ascension.

Fulfillment: Three men who would not bow to Nebuchadnezzar's golden image were bound and cast into a furnace heated seven times hotter, yet they walked loose in the midst of the fire unharmed, the king saw a fourth figure with them, and they came out with not a hair singed and their clothes untouched. The king then blessed their God and decreed that no one speak against Him. Bound, cast into a place of death, preserved alive in it, and brought out unharmed while their persecutor confessed the God who delivered them, the furnace sketches Christ's passage through death and His presence with His people in suffering.
Explanation: TRADITIONAL reading: no New Testament passage calls the furnace a type of Christ, so this is stated as traditional, not explicit. The pattern is in the details, not in a single word: innocent men condemned for refusing false worship, bound and cast into death, a divine companion seen with them in the fire, deliverance without even the smell of fire on their clothes, and a royal confession afterward. It is distinct from the live Daniel entry, which covers the sealed lions' den; this is the companion deliverance, by fire rather than by beasts. The fourth figure Nebuchadnezzar saw is reported as part of the narrative and is not made into a separate Christophany entry.
RelatedPeople: Shadrach; Meshach; Abednego; King Nebuchadnezzar; Jesus
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace

Type: The Son Called Out of Egypt
Fulfillment: God called Israel, His son, out of Egypt at the Exodus, and Matthew says Jesus retraced that path: taken down into Egypt as a child to escape Herod, then called back out, 'that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Out of Egypt have I called my son.' Israel's sonship and exodus were the pattern; Christ, the true Son, recapitulates them.
Explanation: NT-explicit warrant: Matthew 2:15 quotes Hosea 11:1 of Jesus directly. Hosea's words were originally historical, about Israel ('When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt'), which is what makes this typology rather than a forward prediction: the historical pattern of God's son called out of Egypt is fulfilled again, and finally, in Christ. Distinct from the live Red Sea Crossing and Passover Lamb rows, which cover the deliverance itself; this row covers the sonship pattern and the Egypt-to-return movement.
